title: Big bands collapse; Ellington's ASCAP income; working around New York
summary: Edison and Dance discuss why dance halls closed, how Ellington kept going, and Edison's work with Coleman Hawkins and in New York studios.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Yeah. And I just got my -- you know, I just said, if everybody else can do it, I can do it. That's been sort of my philosophy. If I start feeling sorry for myself I say, well, Willie had the same thing happen to them, whoever, and they've come out victorious so how come I can't do it, you know. If anybody else can do something, so can I.
But I can see why that would be a little tragedy.
Because here you'd spent 15 years in big bands. Now here, you'd stayed with Basie and big bands had collapsed.

That's right. That's right. And the one that I really was dependent on, you know. I thought Basie would go on forever, which he will, but there was a lapse in that time, you know. He was broke from the big band. He'd spent a lot of money trying to keep it together. And it just got -- there was no place for a big band to work, see. Because like John Kirby, started the little band playing in the little clubs, you know. And the dance halls were collapsing. The big bands were collapsing, there was no big bands to play in the dance halls.
No. Duke could supplement his thing because --
Yeah, he did. But he did go out with a small band quite a few times. He went to Europe with just Ray
Oh, well that was when he was sick.
Yeah, he went to Europe with just Ray Nance and --
Yeah, you see. And then he had a small group again for a couple times. But his ASCAP ratings kept his band.
Yeah, he'd got enough income to float a while.

Sure. He was paying good salaries in those days, even when the bands were -- I know Johnny Hodges was making five, six hundred dollars a week when we were making $15.00 a night, you know. But it was really disappointing to me when Basie's band broke up. I didn't even know what I was going to do. And I went out with Coleman Hawkins a lot of time, went to Toronto, Cleveland, I played with him, you know. We were good friends.
And I just played with everybody around New York.
Oh, it was a good lesson for me, not to depend on one thing too much because, you know, nothing lasts forever. And be prepared when the worst comes, you know.
Oh, I mean, anything could have happened to the band before that. Basie could have died or --
